Menziesia pilosa is a compact, twiggy, deciduous heath-family shrub with soft blue-green foliage and clusters of small, urn-shaped, yellowish-white to pale pink flowers in late spring that hang beneath the new leaves, giving rise to the common name from their resemblance to tiny hanging bells. Fall color is a soft yellow to orange, and the fine-textured, mounded habit works well in a native rhododendron or azalea understory planting. It is rarely offered in the nursery trade and best grown from local ecotype seed or division by specialty native-plant growers, and it resents heavy clay or poorly drained soils.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; yuzuriha is slow-growing and long-lived, so allow generous room for its eventual size and avoid siting it where later transplanting would be needed.

Daphniphyllum macropodum is a handsome, coarse-textured evergreen shrub or small tree from Japan and Korea grown for its large, glossy, leathery, rhododendron-like leaves carried on distinctive red-tinged petioles, with inconspicuous flowers in spring and small blue-black fruit on female plants. In Japan the new leaves emerge only after the old ones drop, symbolizing generational succession, which gives the plant its common name and traditional use in New Year decorations. It makes a substantial, deer-resistant evergreen backdrop or specimen for a shaded border, tolerating deep shade better than most broadleaf evergreens, and needs little maintenance beyond occasional shaping once established.

planting.note: Plant plugs or container stock in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Appalachian sedge tolerates dry shade and root competition from trees better than most groundcovers, making it a strong turf-grass substitute under mature canopy.

Carex appalachica is an eastern North American native sedge forming a fine-textured, arching, fountain-like mound of hair-thin, dark green leaves that stays neat and low without mowing, spreading gradually by short rhizomes to knit together into a soft, informal lawn alternative. It is one of the most shade- and drought-tolerant of the native fine-leaved sedges, thriving in the dry, root-filled soil beneath oaks and other shade trees where turfgrass struggles, and requires no fertilizer or regular irrigation once established. Space plugs 12 to 18 inches apart for a naturalistic meadow-like planting that fills in within two growing seasons; occasional light shearing in late winter tidies old foliage before spring growth resumes.

Asimina obovata is a Florida-endemic shrub or small tree grown for its large, showy, creamy-white, three-petaled flowers with a sweet fragrance in spring, followed by yellow-green, custard-fleshed fruit smaller than the common pawpaw but edible fresh. Its thick, leathery, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen leaves and drought tolerance make it a distinctive addition to a sandy-soil food forest or native pollinator garden in the Deep South, where it serves as a larval host plant for zebra swallowtail butterflies just as its northern relative does. It needs excellent drainage and full sun to partial shade, tolerates poor, infertile sand, and should never be irrigated on a schedule suited to typical garden shrubs.

Leiophyllum buxifolium is a compact, mounding, evergreen heath-family shrub with tiny, glossy, boxwood-like leaves that bronze attractively in winter, smothered in a profusion of small white to pink star-shaped flowers in mid-spring. Its fine texture and low, tidy habit make it a good substitute for boxwood in acidic-soil gardens, and it works well massed as a foundation planting, in a rock garden, or along a sunny woodland edge. Give it consistently sharp drainage and lean soil, since it is intolerant of wet feet or rich, heavily amended garden beds, and avoid fertilizing beyond a light acidic feeding in spring.
